steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. Explain the difference between RNA and DNA.

steps.action:
Here’s a concise comparison of DNA versus RNA, organized by key features:

1. Chemical Structure  
   • Sugar  
     – DNA: Deoxyribose (lacks a hydroxyl group at the 2′ position)  
     – RNA: Ribose (has a 2′-OH, making it more reactive and less stable)  
   • Nitrogenous Bases  
     – DNA: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)  
     – RNA: Adenine (A), Uracil (U) replaces thymine, Cytosine (C), Guanine (G)  
   • Strand Configuration  
     – DNA: Usually a double helix (two antiparallel strands held by base‐pairing A–T, C–G)  
     – RNA: Typically single‐stranded (but can fold into complex secondary structures via intramolecular base pairing)

2. Functional Roles  
   • DNA  
     – Long‐term storage of genetic information in the nucleus (in eukaryotes) or nucleoid (in prokaryotes)  
     – Template for its own replication prior to cell division  
     – Basis for heredity—passed from parent to offspring  
   • RNA  
     – Messenger RNA (mRNA): Carries coded instructions from DNA to ribosomes  
     – Transfer RNA (tRNA) and ribosomal RNA (rRNA): Key players in translating mRNA into protein  
     – Regulatory RNAs (e.g., microRNA, siRNA): Modulate gene expression  
     – Some RNAs have catalytic activity (“ribozymes”)

3. Stability & Lifespan  
   • DNA  
     – Very stable under physiological conditions; double helix protects bases  
     – Designed for long‐term storage (lifetimes of years to centuries in preserved samples)  
   • RNA  
     – Chemically less stable (2′-OH group promotes hydrolysis)  
     – Turnover can be rapid—minutes to hours—allowing dynamic regulation of gene expression

4. Cellular Localization  
   • DNA  
     – In eukaryotes: confined to nucleus (and mitochondria/chloroplasts)  
     – In prokaryotes: found in the cytoplasmic nucleoid region  
   • RNA  
     – Synthesized in the nucleus (eukaryotes) and exported to the cytoplasm  
     – Performs functions throughout the cell and even extracellularly (e.g., some signaling RNAs)

5. Replication vs. Transcription  
   • DNA Replication  
     – Semi‐conservative: each daughter DNA contains one parental and one new strand  
     – Carried out by DNA polymerases  
   • RNA Transcription  
     – DNA serves as a template for RNA polymerase to synthesize a complementary RNA strand  
     – Only specific regions (genes) are transcribed at any given time

Summary  
DNA is the stable, double‐stranded molecule that stores and transmits genetic information. RNA is the more reactive, generally single‐stranded molecule that translates, regulates and sometimes catalyzes aspects of gene expression. Together, they form the central dogma of molecular biology: DNA → RNA → Protein.
